text: This lesson pulls together everything from this chapter into one workflow: a training job is running slower than it should, and you have to find out why using nvidia-smi, Nsight Systems, and Nsight Compute, then actually fix it.

Start with nvidia-smi dmon while the job runs. If utilization bounces between near-zero and a spike, repeatedly, instead of staying sustained near one hundred percent, the GPU is starved — it's waiting on something else, usually the CPU-side data pipeline, not anything happening on the GPU itself.

If utilization is sustained and high, the bottleneck is on the GPU itself. A Nsight Systems timeline shows what's actually running and whether work that could overlap is instead serialized — a dot item or dot cpu call inside the training loop is a classic culprit, forcing the GPU to finish everything queued before the CPU can read the value.

Once the timeline points at a specific slow kernel, profile just that kernel with Nsight Compute. Its speed-of-light section tells you directly: high memory throughput with low compute throughput means memory-bound, and the reverse means compute-bound — no more guessing from arithmetic intensity by hand.

The fix has to match the diagnosis. A CPU-starved pipeline needs more dataloader workers and pinned memory, not a faster kernel. A memory-bound kernel needs better access patterns or fused operations. A compute-bound kernel is where mixed precision and tensor cores actually help.

Applying a compute-side fix to a kernel the profiler says is memory-bound won't move the needle — always let the limiter verdict decide. Up next, chapter four: working with GPUs in PyTorch, starting with lesson eighteen, device placement in practice.
